_comment: The estimate model: the structure, conversions and physical limits a missing headline is inferred from.
Reviewed like code. build/src/estimates.js reads it; docs/DATA-MODEL.md, 'Estimates', explains it, and
docs/DECISIONS.md D43 records why it replaced D42.
One Gaussian model per headline, on the scale the property varies on. Every piece of evidence in the
snapshot enters it: measured headlines, a material's related measurements (another endpoint, direction,
load or specimen), its other grades, and resin data sheets. Each is first converted to the headline's
own semantics with an offset and a spread, learned from grades that publish both where enough of them
exist and otherwise the documented value (data/tables/conversions.csv, the Estimate columns: D157). The model's structure is polymer identity (inside a
chemical group), reinforcement, reinforcement in a semicrystalline matrix, declared variants and the
test house; for heat deflection of fast-crystallising polymers, the melting point. Each material and
each product adds its own deviation. Every spread that cannot be measured directly is estimated from
the data (empirical Bayes) with the floors below, and the whole model is checked by hiding every
measured headline and predicting it back: the stated coverage is the coverage achieved.

Every spread has a floor, so no fit, and no hold-out refit without a fold of materials, can claim a spread of zero: with TPU and PEBA hidden, an elastomer's product-to-product spread fell to 0.003 and a hold-out claimed near-certainty (DECISIONS D59).
_levelsComment: The likely range is what the tool shows. The plausible range is what may screen a material out of Explore.

tensileStrengthXY._ownCeiling: Not capped: with its floors, a grade's own undescribed strength as a ceiling held the hidden value 71.7 / 88.3 % (likely / plausible), under the 90 % the plausible range must hold; its floors alone 75.0 / 91.7 % (D160).

hdt045._productSpreadByMatrix: A crystalline matrix's products scatter in heat deflection with their crystallinity, far more than a glassy one's: 33.6 °C between filled ones (121 pairs) and 18.9 °C between unfilled ones (31) against 3.1 °C between amorphous ones (5246). One pooled spread, set by the many amorphous pairs, served every matrix and pushed the grade scales to the clamp (D162). Stiffness, strength and stretch keep one spread: a crystalline filled matrix's own stiffness spread (0.149 against 0.267) narrowed its products' ranges below their coverage (likely 54 % against 68 % with the pooled spread).
hdt045._ttm: ttm is fixed, not a floor: the spread of the melting-point slope, °C per 50 °C of melting point

_gradeVariantsComment: A grade declared a variant of its material (grades.csv Variant: a lightweight additive, an undisclosed dense filler) gets its own covariate. One product per variant cannot teach its spread, so the spread is fixed, in the property's scale units, at the top of the grid learned spreads may take: the product's offset is explained by its variant and does not move its polymer family's estimates.

bounds._comment: Physical knowledge of heat deflection. Limits are soft: each is a normal CDF with its own spread, because a melting point or a glass transition plus a margin is itself approximate.
bounds.hdtAboveMelting: A semicrystalline bar cannot hold its shape above its melting point.

amorphousAboveTg.why: An amorphous matrix softens at its glass transition; fibres carry a bar only a little further.

meltingPointSlope.why: Mean rise of HDT at 0.45 MPa per °C of melting point for polymers that crystallise while printing: a fibre-filled bar tracks its melting point (PA6-CF, PA612-CF and PAHT-CF all sit 30 to 40 °C below it); an unfilled bar rises more slowly. The model learns deviations from these slopes, not their sign.

hdtFloor.why: Heat deflection is measured by heating a loaded bar from room temperature (ISO 75, ASTM D648). A bar soft enough to deflect near room temperature has no meaningful HDT, and no filament in the snapshot measures below 48 °C even at 1.8 MPa. A soft floor, so a PE or BVOH estimate cannot reach below freezing.

plausibleValuesSd.why: properties.*.plausibleValues are physical outer limits. They reject impossible observations, and they bound every estimate softly, so a range cannot extend past what the property can physically be.

oneSided.why: A published bound ("> 500 %", "> 16.5 MPa") says the value lies beyond it. In the model it is an observation at the bound with this half-width (in the property's scale), so it informs its family without counting as an exact value; in the material's own estimate it is also a soft limit with this spread, so no range crosses a limit its own grade publishes.

ownVicat.why: Vicat softening (a 10 N needle, 1 mm penetration) is reached at or above HDT at 0.45 MPa for an unfilled bar; the highest Vicat the material's own grades publish caps its unfilled heat deflection estimate softly (BVOH's estimate reached 158 °C against its own Vicat of 90 °C). No melting-point margin is applied below the melting point itself: PVDF publishes 158 °C, 12 °C under its melting point.

density.why: Fibre is denser than any matrix here, so a filled compound cannot be lighter than its polymer except by porosity (filament and printed-part densities sit a few percent below the resin's), nor heavier than the rule of mixtures at the most fibre a printable filament carries: 1/rho = (1 - w)/rho_polymer + w/rho_fibre.

_precisionComment: How a likely range is described, per property: its high-to-low ratio on a log scale, its width in °C for heat deflection. Good: narrow enough to decide on. Fair: indicative. Poor: an order of magnitude only. Elongation of printed parts varies far more than stiffness, so its thresholds are wider.

notApplicable.support: A support product is not characterised as a structural material. Its values are shown only where its own sources publish them.

fitting._comment: Judgements the fit makes, reviewed here rather than buried in code (build/src/estimate/). Numerical method settings (the hyperparameter grid, the quantile integration) stay in code.
fitting.documentedPairsWhy: A documented conversion offset counts as this many grades publishing both kinds, so a few odd pairs refine it and cannot overturn it.
fitting.minPairsForSpreadWhy: A conversion's spread is learned (MAD of the pairs) only from at least this many pairs; below it the documented spread stands.
fitting.keepKindsWithinSpreadWhy: On each product only the most direct related kinds are kept: those whose conversion spread is within this factor of the tightest. Stacking a flexural and a break strength double-counted one test house's ratio.
fitting.minBetweenProductPairsWhy: The spread between two products of one material is measured directly once this many same-material pairs exist; below it, it is estimated with the other spreads.
fitting.conflictWhy: An observation whose leave-one-out residual exceeds conflictZ standard deviations has its noise variance multiplied by conflictNoiseFactor (its spread by 5), at most conflictPasses times, and is reported. A material's only evidence for a headline is never down-weighted.
fitting.severalMakersWhy: A conversion that learns from several makers (conversions.csv Estimate learns "pairs, several makers": the annealed kinds) keeps its documented offset and spread until at least 5 pairs from at least 2 makers publish both kinds. Three PPA pairs of one maker (Siraya Tech, +101 to +108 °C) once taught the annealed heat deflection −77 °C for every crystalline matrix, where a hot-printed nylon or PPS is already crystalline and gains far less (D167).
fitting.spreadSampleMaxWhy: The spread search sees at most this many observations: every measured headline, then the rest one material at a time in turn. A search is hundreds of fits and a fit is cubic in what it sees, so this is where the stage's cost is. The posterior, the calibration and the screening back-test still see every observation. At 400 the searched spreads match a search on everything to within 0.02 of a scale unit (DECISIONS D77).

calibration._comment: How the likely and plausible ranges are scaled to hold hidden measured headlines as often as they claim, and when the build refuses the result.
calibration.foldsWhy: Every hold-out (calibration and the screening back-test) predicts a material with spreads fitted without its fold of materials, one fold in this many, so the ranges are judged on what the fit never saw.
calibration.scaleWhy: With at least minHeld hidden headlines, each range's scale is the observed quantile of the standardised errors over the nominal one, clamped to the interval given; with fewer, defaultScale.
calibration.outlierWhy: A measured headline more than outlierZ calibrated plausible standard deviations from its prediction is listed (EST-OUTLIER) for a reviewer.
calibration.toleranceWhy: The build fails if the likely range's coverage drifts more than likelyTolerance from its level, or the plausible range's coverage falls more than plausibleShortfall below its level (EST-CALIBRATION).

screening._comment: An estimate never passes a material. In Explore it may screen one out when the range it screens on wholly fails a requirement and no printed measurement of the material bounds the headline to meet it (headline_definitions.csv Lower bound). Each end of that range is set by the back-test every build runs (DECISIONS D59, build/src/estimate/screening.js).
screening.why: Each end of an evidence class's screening ranges is a distribution-free tolerance limit of where the honestly predicted true values of that class fell: a new true value lies beyond it at most maxWrongRate of the time, with this confidence. It is never inside the plausible range shown, and moves outwards only where the back-test shows the model's tail is too thin. Setting a limit at all takes 22 back-tested cases at 10% and 90%. How often a true value lies beyond an end bounds how often a screen on it is wrong, since a screen is wrong only when the requirement also lies between the end and the true value.
